text:
Donald Knuth was born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and earned his Bachelor of Science and Master of Science degrees from Case Institute of Technology in 1960 before completing his PhD in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in 1963. His academic career included positions at Caltech and Burroughs Corporation, where he made significant contributions to compiler design, such as influencing the development of the DEFINE symbol in Burroughs ALGOL. In 1969, he joined the faculty of Stanford University as the Fletcher Jones Professor of Computer Science, eventually becoming Professor Emeritus of The Art of Computer Programming in 1993. Knuth is best known for his monumental seven-volume series, *The Art of Computer Programming* (TAoCP), which he began publishing in 1968 with the goal of providing a comprehensive and rigorous foundation for the discipline. He also co-authored *Concrete Mathematics* with Ronald Graham and Oren Patashnik, a text designed to teach computer science students the necessary mathematical tools.
Beyond his technical work, Knuth is celebrated for his humor and unique personal style, including his famous reward for finding typographical errors in his books and his satirical creation of "iTeX." He received numerous prestigious awards throughout his life, including the Turing Award in 1974, the National Medal of Science in 1979, and the ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award in 1971. Knuth was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1975, the National Academy of Engineering in 1981, and the American Philosophical Society in 2012. He was also recognized as a Fellow of the British Computer Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the American Mathematical Society. His legacy is further honored by Asteroid 21656, named in his honor in 2001, and his profound influence on the fields of algorithms, typesetting (via TeX and Metafont), and computer science education.
